stem:
You are to plan an experiment to find out which dyes are present in the coloured coating of a brand of sweets, and whether they are among four permitted dyes, P, Q, R and S, which are available as pure solids.

The coating can be dissolved off the sweets with a small volume of water. Thin-layer chromatography plates (silica, with a fluorescent indicator) and a suitable solvent are available. The solvent is flammable and harmful by inhalation.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain how the experiment will show which dyes are present.

points.description: The dyes in the coating separate because each has a different attraction to the silica (stationary phase) and solubility in the solvent, so each has a different Rf value
A dye in the coating is identified by matching its Rf (or spot position) with that of a pure reference dye run on the same plate

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Each dye is held to a different extent by the polar silica and dissolves to a different extent in the solvent, so the dyes in the coating separate into spots with different Rf values. A spot from the coating that travels the same distance (same Rf) as one of the pure dyes on the same plate is probably that dye.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State the variables that must be kept the same for the Rf values to be compared, and explain why the samples are run on the same plate.

points.description: Same solvent, same type of plate, same temperature (and covered, saturated tank)
Running on one plate means all samples experience exactly the same conditions and solvent front, so distances can be compared directly

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The solvent, the type of plate and the temperature must be the same, with the tank covered so the air is saturated with solvent vapour. Running all samples side by side on one plate guarantees identical conditions and one solvent front, so positions can be compared directly.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Reference solutions of each dye are to be made at 0.50 g dm⁻³. Calculate the mass of dye, in mg, needed to make 10.0 cm³ of one solution.
parts.explanation: Mass = 0.50 g dm⁻³ × 0.0100 dm³ = 5.0 × 10⁻³ g = 5.0 mg. Multiplying 0.50 by 10.0 without converting cm³ to dm³ gives 5.0 g.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Mass = 0.50 g dm⁻³ × 0.0100 dm³ = 5.0 × 10⁻³ g = 5.0 mg. Multiplying 0.50 by 10.0 without converting cm³ to dm³ gives 5.0 g.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe the method in numbered steps, naming the apparatus.

points.description: Dissolve the coating from a few sweets in a small volume (about 1-2 cm³) of water in a small beaker or test tube; make the reference solutions

Draw a pencil baseline about 1.5 cm from the bottom of the TLC plate; use capillary tubes to apply small spots of the coating solution and of P, Q, R and S along it, letting each dry (re-spot to concentrate)
Place the plate in a tank containing solvent to a depth below the baseline; cover with a lid; leave until the solvent has risen most of the way

Remove the plate, mark the solvent front in pencil at once, dry it (in a fume cupboard) and view under UV light (or note coloured spots); measure distances to the centre of each spot and calculate Rf values

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: 1. Dissolve the coating from three sweets in about 2 cm³ of water; make up 0.50 g dm⁻³ solutions of P, Q, R and S. 2. Draw a pencil baseline 1.5 cm from the bottom of a TLC plate and, using fine capillary tubes, place small spots of each solution 1 cm apart, drying between applications. 3. Stand the plate in a covered tank with solvent about 0.5 cm deep (below the baseline) and leave until the solvent is about 1 cm from the top. 4. Remove the plate, mark the solvent front immediately in pencil, dry it in a fume cupboard, and view the spots (in daylight and under UV light). Measure each distance from the baseline to the centre of the spot and calculate Rf values.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State one safety precaution, linked to a hazard.

points.description: The solvent is flammable and harmful by inhalation: no naked flames and use a fume cupboard (or do not look directly at UV light: use UV goggles)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The solvent is flammable and harmful if inhaled, so keep it away from flames and run and dry the plate in a fume cupboard.

points.description: Columns: sample; distance moved by spot / cm; distance moved by solvent front / cm; Rf (no unit), with a row for each spot

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Columns: sample (coating spot 1, 2 …, P, Q, R, S) | distance moved by spot / cm | distance moved by solvent front / cm | Rf.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: In a trial, a spot from the coating moved 3.3 cm and the solvent front 7.5 cm. Calculate its Rf value, to two decimal places.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: A coating spot has the same Rf as dye Q. Suggest how to make the identification more certain, and explain why this is needed.

points.description: Repeat the chromatogram with a different solvent (or a co-spot of coating mixed with Q) and check the spots still match / merge into one
Two different dyes can have the same Rf in one solvent by coincidence

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Run the chromatogram again with a different solvent, and spot a mixture of the coating solution and Q: if the spot still matches Q and the mixture gives a single spot, the identification is much more likely to be correct. This is needed because different dyes can have the same Rf in one solvent.

explanation: Separate by TLC and match Rf values with pure dyes on the same plate; 10.0 cm³ of 0.50 g dm⁻³ needs 5.0 mg; trial Rf 0.44; confirm with a second solvent.
hints: Rf = distance of spot ÷ distance of solvent front.
Convert cm³ to dm³ when using g dm⁻³.

stem:
You are to plan an experiment to find the percentage by mass of caffeine in tea leaves grown in the Eastern Highlands.

Caffeine dissolves in hot water. After the leaves are boiled with water and sodium carbonate and the mixture is filtered and cooled, caffeine can be extracted from the aqueous solution with dichloromethane, which is immiscible with water and denser than it. Dichloromethane is volatile and harmful. Assume the partition coefficient Kpc(dichloromethane/water) for caffeine is 8.0.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why dichloromethane is a suitable solvent for this extraction.

points.description: It is immiscible with water, so two layers form and can be separated
Caffeine is more soluble in it than in water (Kpc > 1), and it is volatile, so it can be evaporated off easily to leave the caffeine

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Dichloromethane does not mix with water, so it forms a separate layer that can be run off. Caffeine is more soluble in it than in water (Kpc = 8.0), and because it is volatile it can be evaporated easily, leaving the caffeine.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: 100 cm³ of the aqueous tea extract contains 0.250 g of caffeine. Calculate the total mass of caffeine, in g, removed by two successive extractions with 25.0 cm³ portions of dichloromethane.
parts.explanation: Fraction left after each extraction = 100 ÷ (100 + 8.0 × 25.0) = 0.333; left after two = 0.250 × (0.333)² = 0.0278 g; extracted = 0.222 g. One 50.0 cm³ portion would remove only 0.200 g.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Fraction left after each extraction = 100 ÷ (100 + 8.0 × 25.0) = 0.333; left after two = 0.250 × (0.333)² = 0.0278 g; extracted = 0.222 g. One 50.0 cm³ portion would remove only 0.200 g.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Describe the method in numbered steps, including quantities and apparatus.

points.description: Weigh about 8-10 g of tea leaves accurately (to 0.01 g); boil with about 100 cm³ of water and some sodium carbonate for a fixed time (e.g. 15 minutes); filter and cool the solution
Shake the cooled solution with a 25 cm³ portion of dichloromethane in a stoppered separating funnel, venting through the tap; allow layers to separate
Run off the lower dichloromethane layer; repeat with further fresh portions (at least two) and combine the extracts; dry with anhydrous sodium sulfate (or magnesium sulfate) and filter
Evaporate the dichloromethane in a weighed evaporating basin (warm water bath, fume cupboard) and weigh the residue (repeat to constant mass) to find the mass of caffeine

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: 1. Weigh about 8 g of tea leaves to 0.01 g, and boil them with 100 cm³ of water and 2 g of sodium carbonate for 15 minutes; filter and cool. 2. Pour the filtrate into a separating funnel with 25 cm³ of dichloromethane, stopper, shake gently and vent through the tap; let the layers separate. 3. Run the lower dichloromethane layer into a flask; repeat with two more 25 cm³ portions and combine the extracts. Dry them with anhydrous sodium sulfate and filter into a weighed evaporating basin. 4. Evaporate the solvent on a warm water bath in a fume cupboard, then weigh the basin and residue, repeating until the mass is constant.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Give two safety precautions, each linked to a hazard.

points.description: Dichloromethane is volatile and harmful: work in a fume cupboard / avoid inhaling; wear gloves
Pressure builds up in the separating funnel when shaking a volatile solvent: vent frequently through the tap (or hot liquids: handle with care, wear eye protection)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Dichloromethane is harmful and volatile, so use it in a fume cupboard and wear gloves and eye protection. Its vapour builds up pressure in the separating funnel, so the funnel must be vented regularly through the tap.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: From 8.00 g of tea leaves, 0.188 g of crude caffeine was obtained. Calculate the percentage by mass of caffeine in the leaves.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Suggest one reason why the percentage found may be too high and one reason why it may be too low, with an improvement for one of them.

points.description: Too high: the crude caffeine contains impurities (other extracted compounds such as pigments, or solvent not fully evaporated/wet)
Too low: incomplete extraction (too few portions) or loss during transfers; improvement: more extractions with fresh solvent, or recrystallise the product and check purity by TLC or melting point

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The value may be too high because the crude solid contains other extracted substances or traces of solvent; it may be too low because extraction was incomplete or some caffeine was lost in transfers. Using more portions of fresh solvent, heating to constant mass, and recrystallising the product (checking its purity by TLC or melting point) would improve the result.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: State the measurements that must be recorded.

points.description: Mass of tea leaves; mass of empty evaporating basin; mass of basin + caffeine (repeated to constant mass)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The mass of tea leaves used, the mass of the empty evaporating basin, and the mass of the basin with the dried caffeine (to constant mass).

explanation: Dichloromethane is immiscible and dissolves caffeine well; two 25 cm³ portions remove 0.222 g of 0.250 g; caffeine 2.35% by mass of the leaves.
hints: Fraction left per extraction = V_aq ÷ (V_aq + Kpc × V_org).
Percentage = mass of caffeine ÷ mass of leaves × 100.
